papers.title: Real-Time Krylov Theory for Quantum Computing Algorithms

false_alarm.note: Cited for why ill-conditioned generalized eigenproblems are numerically unstable, which is the cited work's subject (condition numbers and backward error of GEPs); the truncation rule itself is the citing authors' method.

Caused by the checker: the reference is a 2020 Springer workshop volume ('Orthogonal Polynomials: 2nd AIMS-Volkswagen Stiftung Workshop'), but the resolver matched the generic title to a different survey called 'Orthogonal Polynomials', which was then checked.
Identification citation: quantum phase estimation cited to the standard textbook, which presents the algorithm. Requiring the words 'Hamiltonian diagonalization' is too literal.
Childs and Wiebe do give the success probability of LCU; 'where Ex specifies the center of spectral decay' is the citing paper's own notation for its application, not a claim about the source.

Filter diagonalization (small Hamiltonian matrix built from real-time-propagated states) is exactly the classical ancestor of solving generalized eigenproblems from real-time evolution; cited in a group of four. 'Possibly the wrong reference' is wrong.

debatable.note: The cited work analyses the success and failure probability of LCU constructions; the 'flagged state' and 'target amplitude' framing is the citing paper's own application.

papers.title: The Medical Segmentation Decathlon

false_alarm.note: Caused by the checker: the per-dataset targets (17 in total) are in a table of the cited data paper, and the checker's text of cited papers omits table contents.
The cited LiTS paper lists IRCAD in France as a data source and describes the LiTS data used for the Decathlon's liver task; the hospital's full name is a detail, not a misattribution.
The cited paper describes an 'unmanageable number of research papers' and about 12,000 studies building on U-Net since 2015, i.e. thousands per year; the not-found verdict is too literal.

debatable.note: The checker read the 2019 arXiv preprint ('29 out of 49'); the sentence cites the 2021 Nature Methods version, whose updated results likely contain the 33-of-53 figure. The BraTS 2020 win is not in the preprint either. Version mismatch, not verifiable here.
The preprint the checker read says the KiTS top-15 were U-Net offspring but gives no count of nnU-Net derivatives; the journal version may. Same version mismatch.
The GlaS paper says malignant gland boundaries are not well defined and that inter-observer variability was not measured; 'experts often do not agree' is a stretch, cited jointly with another work.
The source says 70% of challenge tasks were segmentation; the sentence says 70% of challenges. A real but minor imprecision (challenges can have several tasks).
The sentence describes the citing paper's own challenge; the citation most plausibly supports the notion of a challenge 'task', which the cited meta-analysis defines, not the MSD details.

papers.title: On the evolution of the size of Lyman alpha halos across cosmic time: no change in the circumgalactic gas distribution when probed by line emission

genuine.note: Cited for seeing no redshift evolution, but the cited paper reports a significant decrease of halo scale lengths towards higher redshift (factor 2 between z~3.7 and 5.1).
Cited as the first to stack narrow-band images of LBGs, but the cited paper itself credits Hayashino et al. (2004) with an earlier stacked narrow-band Lyα study of LBGs in SSA22.
The cited KCWI study measures 15.6 kpc for its median stack and attributes 17.5 kpc to an earlier narrow-band study; the citing sentence credits it with 17.5 kpc.

false_alarm.note: Partly caused by the checker: the LaTeX converter dropped '≲' so 'z ≲ 0.2' reached the judge as 'redshift 0.2'; the source's 0.028-0.18 and radius ratios of 1-3.6 (Hα) and ~2.9 (FUV) support 'z ≲ 0.2' and '1 to 4 times'.
Co-cited with [24], which carries the numbers; this work confirms Lyα is more extended than the FUV.
The judge's own explanation says the source supports larger ratios (median 10.8, 4 to >20) than the 2-4 found at low z.
The source describes the limited HST field of view and Lyα extents of typically 10 kpc; the sentence is a fair summary.
The median 4.5 kpc halo is supported; 'can only probe 2 scale lengths' is the citing authors' own calculation.

Caused by the checker: the DOI is Duval et al. 2016 (Lyα escape from the edge-on galaxy Mrk 1486), but the arXiv-preprint lookup matched the generic title 'The Lyman alpha reference sample' to a different LARS paper (Puschnig et al.) and checked that text.
The judge's own explanation says the source's points scatter around a 10:1 ratio (median 10.8).
Starburst99 models show ionizing photon output peaking in the first few Myr and falling by orders of magnitude for old populations; the sentence is a fair reading of the models.
The source gives 1.0-18.7 kpc with a median of 4.5 kpc; the judge's own explanation says it matches. Rounding 18.7 to 18 is not number drift.
'[similar to 32, 18]' identifies comparable galaxy samples; the claim about non-cospatial diagnostics is the citing authors' own conclusion, not attributed to these works.
As for [18]: the citation identifies similar compact galaxies, not the source of the conclusion.

The judge compared against the ~40 kpc extent from the previous sentence; the MUSE scale lengths (median ~4.5 kpc) are similar to the 5-8 kpc this work finds in some subsamples, exactly as the sentence says.
Scale lengths of 5-10 kpc are similar to the MUSE results; the cited work does not need to mention MUSE (the comparison is the citing authors').
Same as [49]: the cited scale lengths are comparable to MUSE; the comparison is the citing authors'.

debatable.note: The source describes only a 'slight advantage' for the adjacent long-pass configuration and notes the same drawbacks remain; 'more effective' is a mild overstatement.
This LARS paper (dust and scattering) does not state that UV/Hα knots are absent in Lyα or that Lyα is smoother; that finding is reported elsewhere in the LARS series.
Joint summary of three surveys; COS-GASS probes 63-231 kpc, so 'as far as 300 kpc' overstates its reach, but the general statement about extended H I halos is supported.
Same joint summary; COS-Burst sightlines reach roughly the virial radius (~230 kpc), not 300 kpc.
Same joint summary; COS-Halos finds ~1 Å Lyα equivalent widths out to 150 kpc, which supports strong extended absorption but not 300 kpc.
The 25th percentile of the MUSE sample's UV magnitudes is not stated in the text; it may be derived from the published catalogue.
The upper brightness limit of the LBG sample is not stated as such; likely derived from the sample's properties.
Co-cited with the Mrk 1486 paper; this morphology paper discusses orientation effects but does not single out Mrk 1486.
The source gives a median ratio of 10.8, not a mean of 12; a mean computed from its catalogue may well be 12, but it is not stated.

Both describe a bright central component plus a flatter outer component; the source calls the outskirts exponential discs while the citing paper says 'not exponential', so the 'similar results' are similar only loosely.
Group citation [65, 39, 40]: the 1-18 kpc range and 4.5 kpc median come from [39]; this work reports 1-7 kpc, which fits inside the range.
The source quotes per-Å surface-brightness limits (2.8 and 5.5 × 10^-20); integrated over a narrow band these are of order 10^-19, so 'very similar' is loose but defensible.
LARS II reports mostly low escape fractions with five galaxies above 10%; calling a 12% mean 'quite comparable' is a judgement call.

papers.title: Perinatal care in Western Uganda: Prevalence and factors associated with appropriate care among women attending three district hospitals

false_alarm.note: The source states the stillbirth target as a global average of 8 per 1000 total births; 'less than 8' is a wording nuance of the same SDG/ENAP target, cited as part of a group [1-3].

Caused by the checker: the PDF splits the reference's DOI across a line break ('journal.pmed. 1002151'), the truncated DOI resolved to an unrelated tuberculosis review, and that wrong paper was flagged as off-topic. The real reference (Leslie et al., PLoS Med 2016) was never checked.

debatable.note: 64.1% and 24.7% do not appear in the cited Nepal study's text, but the checker's text of cited papers omits table contents, and the proportions may be in a table or derived from one.

The cited Ethiopian study says care quality 'might differ' with equipment, workload and provider commitment; the sentence's 'common occurrences in low income countries' is the citing authors' generalisation, cited jointly with [30].

Supply-chain strengthening is supported; the cited paper (northern Uganda scale-up) describes renovating specific operating theatres, not upgrading public and private facilities for clean and safe delivery in the region.

papers.title: Primaquine in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency: an adaptive pharmacometric assessment of ascending dose regimens in healthy volunteers

false_alarm.note: The weekly regimen is a single 0.75 mg/kg (about 45 mg) dose each week; 28% of G6PD-deficient patients had a >25% haemoglobin fall by day 7 (after the first dose) and one needed transfusion, which supports 'may not be safe'.
Definition citation: the CPIC/DPWG consensus defines the activity score and phenotype for *10/*10 (intermediate metaboliser); the 8/27 frequency is the citing study's own result.

The cited study reports significant, mostly transient haemoglobin falls after the first weekly dose, and contrasts the weekly regimen's smaller drops with daily dosing; the sentence paraphrases it fairly.

The cited meta-analysis states that primaquine compounds the haemoglobin reduction, particularly in G6PD deficiency, which is the context of the sentence; the 'not predictable in G6PD-normal patients' objection misses that context.
Data-source citation: the Cambodian study is the dataset of vivax patients given 45 mg (0.75 mg/kg) primaquine doses that the model used.
This is the modelling paper itself, and it explicitly uses the Cambodian vivax-patient data; the objection that the population is not stated as vivax patients is wrong.
Method citation for the CYP2D6 genotyping protocol, which the cited paper describes; the haemoglobin electrophoresis in the same sentence is the citing study's own procedure.

The Papua audit shows vivax malaria (a relapsing infection) causing deaths, with extreme anaemia the commonest cause and young children at high risk; cited jointly with a meta-analysis. 'Relapsing' and 'higher transmission settings' are context, not unsupported claims.
The meta-analysis states vivax is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality and that relapses compound anaemia; the child-mortality part is carried by the co-cited audit.

debatable.note: The cited meta-analysis supports a high total dose of about 7 mg/kg versus 3.5 mg/kg; the lower bound of '5 to 7 mg/kg' is not stated in it.

papers.title: Respected but stigmatized: Healthcare workers caring for COVID-19 patients

genuine.note: The cited study never defines stigma; it only lists manifestations (e.g. 'prejudice (devaluation of HCWs)') that it attributes to its own references [7, 8]. The general definition is not in the cited work.
The cited Jordanian survey of depression and anxiety never mentions stigma (no occurrence in the full text), so it cannot support 'stigmatization can impact the mental health of HCWs'.

false_alarm.note: The cited interview study says stigma 'still poses a threat to mental well-being' of hospital doctors. Doctors are healthcare workers; flagging the claim as broader than the source is pedantic.

debatable.note: The cited work reports (citing another study) that perceived stigma is associated with anxiety and depression; PTSD and suicide are absent, but the sentence cites two works [10, 11] for that list, and 'can lead to' over an association is a mild overstatement.
